splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year or whether actuaries may adopt assumptions after that date. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing plans to use more current information in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: Trustees of IAM National Pension Fund v. M & K Employee Solutions

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, so the term does not run during the period of absconding, extending the court's authority.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled by absconding, as no statutory provision authorizes courts to extend the term beyond what the judgment specifies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether the gatekeeping provision of § 2244(b)(1), which categorically bars claims previously presented in habeas, applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions. If it applies, federal prisoners face a stricter barrier than Congress may have intended; if not, they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on previously raised claims in § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to challenge election rules before an election takes place. If standing is granted broadly, pre-election challenges to voting procedures would be far easier to bring; if denied, disputes would be concentrated post-election. The split affects rules on mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and election administration nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office have Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to state election laws affecting ballot counting procedures.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to challenge state ballot-counting rules pre-election because the alleged injury is too speculative or generalized.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps judicial deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations in criminal or quasi-criminal sentencing contexts.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the rule of lenity should take precedence over deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary (under Kisor/Stinson) when interpreting ambiguous sentencing guidelines provisions. At least three circuits hold lenity trumps deference, while others (including the Third Circuit) have held that deference prevails. The issue has taken on greater significance after Loper Bright overruled Chevron.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity should prevail over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal or sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that Kisor/Stinson deference to the Sentencing Commission's authoritative commentary takes priority over lenity when interpreting ambiguous guidelines provisions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' means 'and' or 'or' in the safety-valve provision. The Ninth and Eleventh Circuits hold defendants must meet all three criteria to be disqualified, while the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits hold that any one criterion is disqualifying. This split leads to dramatically different mandatory minimum sentences depending on jurisdiction.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its natural conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as distributive or disjunctive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, based on Application Note 1's expansion of the guideline text.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds conspiracy and attempt to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor. Some circuits defer to the commentary and include inchoate offenses, while others hold the guideline text is unambiguous and does not cover conspiracy or attempt. The Commission has since amended the guideline text, but the split remains relevant for cases sentenced under prior versions.

positions.label: Inchoate offenses included via commentary deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is entitled to deference as the Commission's authoritative interpretation, and conspiracy and attempt qualify as controlled substance offenses under the career-offender guideline.

positions.label: Inchoate offenses excluded — text is unambiguous
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text of § 4B1.2(b) is unambiguous and does not include inchoate offenses, so Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition and is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule criminalizes substances not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires that the underlying substance be federally scheduled, or whether any state-scheduled substance suffices. The Eighth Circuit holds there is no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation onto the guideline, while other circuits require federal scheduling. The Supreme Court's decision in Brown v. United States addressed a related but distinct statutory question.

positions.label: State schedule suffices
positions.summary: Holds that a conviction under state law qualifies as a controlled substance offense even if the substance is not on the federal schedules, because the guideline text refers broadly to 'state law' offenses.

positions.label: Federal schedule required
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction is a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance is also federally scheduled, because the Guidelines should be read in light of the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose a sentence upon revocation of supervised release to punish the defendant for the violation, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to the purposes of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether sentences imposed upon revocation of supervised release may serve a punitive purpose. The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for supervised release violations, while other circuits hold that revocation sentences should focus on the breach of trust and cannot be imposed primarily to punish. This affects hundreds of revocation proceedings annually.

positions.label: Punitive purpose permitted
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violating conditions of supervised release when imposing revocation sentences.

positions.label: Punitive purpose not permitted
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences must focus on the defendant's breach of trust and the court's interest in the defendant's rehabilitation, not punishment for the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in law — particularly the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory consecutive 25-year sentences for stacked § 924(c) counts — can support compassionate release. Some circuits hold such changes may contribute to extraordinary and compelling circumstances, while others (like the Seventh and Eighth Circuits) hold they cannot. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to resolve this, but circuits differ on whether it exceeds the Commission's authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, alone or in combination with other factors, may constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, as this would circumvent Congress's decision not to make the change retroactive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of imprisonment) must proceed via habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or may use civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens), and whether habeas is the exclusive remedy for such claims.
splits.description: Since Preiser v. Rodriguez, circuits have developed an unresolved conflict over whether challenges to conditions or terms of confinement — as distinct from the fact or duration of imprisonment — must be brought as habeas petitions or may proceed as civil rights actions. This longstanding split affects prisoners' access to federal courts, particularly when challenging BOP decisions about custody classification, transfer to prerelease facilities, or earned time credits under the First Step Act.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive or primary remedy
positions.summary: Holds that challenges affecting the execution of a sentence, including transfer to prerelease custody, must be brought as habeas petitions under § 2241 rather than civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights actions also available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may challenge conditions of confinement through civil rights actions and are not limited to habeas, as habeas exclusivity applies only to challenges to the fact or duration of confinement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is governed by the civil 30-day deadline or the criminal 14-day deadline under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the 30-day appeal deadline) or part of the criminal proceeding (triggering the 14-day deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies, but at least one circuit has applied the criminal deadline.

positions.label: Civil deadline (30 days) applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under FRAP 4(a) governs.

positions.label: Criminal deadline (14 days) applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion arises in a criminal case and is governed by the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under FRAP 4(b).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's property belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether post-petition appreciation in property value inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor after a good-faith Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 conversion. The Ninth Circuit held that appreciation belongs to the estate based on § 541(a)'s broad definition of estate property, while other courts have reached the opposite conclusion, reading § 348(f)(1)(A) as protecting debtors' post-petition gains to encourage Chapter 13 filings.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7, based on § 541(a)'s broad definition of estate property.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor upon good-faith conversion, consistent with § 348(f)'s purpose of encouraging Chapter 13 filings by protecting debtors from losing post-petition gains.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal medical records in litigation is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine of 28 U.S.C. § 1291.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denial of a motion to seal documents referencing medical treatments and diagnoses is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a 'value of high order' that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment. Other circuits have not uniformly recognized this category of orders as immediately appealable, creating a potential divergence in appellate jurisdiction standards.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal medical records are immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of high order effectively lost if review is delayed.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denials of motions to seal generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements, as the interest in confidentiality can be addressed through other protective measures or post-judgment review.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the Second Circuit's approach to legal standards for discrimination claims in hospitality settings, indicating that lower courts have applied divergent standards. The decision could affect hospitality, retail, and service industries nationwide by establishing clearer rules for fair treatment and damages.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Applies broader standards for proving discrimination in places of public accommodation, potentially lowering the threshold for establishing liability.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Applies more restrictive standards for discrimination claims against business operators, requiring stronger showings of intentional or systemic discrimination.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
